solution.concept_anchor: Tests for severability — textual, substantial, policy

statement_analysis.statement: A court applying the doctrine of severability will strike down only the unconstitutional portion of a law if that portion is grammatically and textually separable from the rest of the enactment.
statement_analysis.reason: Textual severability is the first and most basic test — if the offending provision can be physically excised without doing violence to the grammatical structure of the remaining provisions, severability is possible.

statement_analysis.statement: Even if an unconstitutional provision is textually separable from the rest of an Act, it must still be struck down with the entire Act if the legislature would not have enacted the valid portion independently of the invalid portion.
statement_analysis.reason: The policy (or legislative intent) test for severability asks whether the legislature would have enacted the surviving portion alone. If the answer is no — because the valid and invalid portions form an inseverable legislative scheme — the entire Act falls, even if textual separation was possible.

statement_analysis.statement: Under the doctrine of severability, once a court determines that a provision is textually separable, the remaining portions of the Act are automatically upheld without any further constitutional examination.
statement_analysis.reason: Textual severability is necessary but not sufficient. Courts also examine substantial severability (does the remaining portion make legal sense without the excised part?) and policy severability (would the legislature have passed the remainder alone?). All tests must be satisfied before the remainder is upheld.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know that severability involves textual separability may assume all three statements are correct without noting that Statement 3 oversimplifies by making textual separability sufficient alone.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — textual separability is a valid and recognised test for severability. Statement 1 is correct.

Confirm Statement 2 — the legislative intent/policy test means textual separability alone is not sufficient; if the legislature wouldn't have passed the valid parts alone, the whole falls. Statement 2 is correct.

Test Statement 3 — the phrase 'automatically upheld without any further constitutional examination' is the trap. Textual separability is only the first test; substantial and policy severability must also be satisfied. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 contains a partial truth embedded in an overstatement. Textual separability IS a valid test, and IS a necessary condition — but the statement adds 'automatically upheld without any further constitutional examination', converting a necessary condition into a sufficient one. Students who know that severability requires textual separation (and nothing more, in their simplified understanding) will mark Statement 3 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
The doctrine of severability has multiple tests that must all be considered before a court decides to save or strike down the remaining portions of a partially unconstitutional law.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Textual severability asks whether the unconstitutional provision can be excised as text without grammatically destroying the rest of the enactment. This is the foundational and first test.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The policy/legislative intent test asks a counterfactual — would Parliament have passed the valid portions alone, knowing the unconstitutional provision would be absent? If not, the entire law falls. This is established in R.M.D. Chamarbaugwala v. Union of India (1957).
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Textual separability is a necessary but not sufficient condition. Courts must additionally apply the substantial severability test (whether the remaining law makes meaningful sense) and the policy test (whether the legislature would have passed the remainder alone). The word 'automatically' in Statement 3 makes it incorrect.

Value Addition:
• The doctrine of severability is applied consistently across Article 13 (void laws) and Article 14 (arbitrary classification) challenges.
• A classic example: a law regulating both lotteries and games of skill. If the lottery provision violates a fundamental right, the skill-game portion may survive if the tests are met.
• Courts prefer saving valid portions over striking down entire laws — in keeping with the presumption of constitutionality.

solution.concept_anchor: 24th Amendment — inserting Article 13(4) to nullify Golak Nath
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know Article 13(4) was inserted to deal with constitutional amendments may guess it was the 42nd Amendment (which made many other major changes to fundamental rights) rather than the 24th.
elimination_logic: Identify what Article 13(4) does: it declares that constitutional amendments under Article 368 shall not be deemed 'law' under Article 13, directly nullifying the Golak Nath holding.
The Golak Nath verdict was delivered in 1967. Parliament's response came in 1971 through the 24th Amendment, not the 42nd (1976) or the 25th (1971, which did a different thing — Article 31-C).
Eliminate (a) — the 42nd Amendment (1976) expanded Article 31-C; it did not insert Article 13(4).
Eliminate (b) — the 25th Amendment (1971) inserted Article 31-C; it did not insert Article 13(4).
Eliminate (d) — the 44th Amendment (1978) restored judicial review protections; it did not insert Article 13(4).
Option (c) — the 24th Constitutional Amendment (1971) inserted Article 13(4) to counteract Golak Nath. Correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal-swap trap works because multiple amendments in the 1971–1976 period affected the FRs-amendment relationship. Students who know that 'an amendment inserted Article 13(4)' but are not precise about which one will be pulled toward the 42nd Amendment (the most famous Emergency-era constitutional change) or toward the 25th Amendment (which also dealt with FRs). Only the 24th Amendment inserted Article 13(4).
solution.final_explanation:
Article 13(4) was a targeted parliamentary response to a specific Supreme Court verdict.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment (1976) made far-reaching changes including adding Fundamental Duties and modifying Article 31-C's scope. It did not insert Article 13(4).
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The 25th Constitutional Amendment (1971) inserted Article 31-C, allowing laws implementing Articles 39(b) and (c) to override Articles 14 and 19. It did not insert Article 13(4).
• Option (c) — Correct: The 24th Constitutional Amendment (1971) inserted Article 13(4) specifically to overrule Golak Nath v. State of Punjab. Golak Nath had held that constitutional amendments are 'law' under Article 13 and cannot abridge fundamental rights. Article 13(4) declares that amendments under Article 368 shall not be deemed 'law' for Article 13 purposes.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) made several corrections to Emergency-era changes but did not insert Article 13(4) — that was already in place.

Value Addition:
• The 24th Amendment also made it mandatory for the President to give assent to Constitution Amendment Bills.
• Kesavananda Bharati (1973) later rendered the Golak Nath vs. 24th Amendment debate somewhat academic by introducing the Basic Structure doctrine.
• The 24th Amendment also clarified that Article 368 confers power to amend any provision of the Constitution.

solution.concept_anchor: Ajay Hasia factors — instrumentality of State test under Article 12
solution.strong_distractor: b — The Sukhdev Singh case is a real and important case about corporations and Article 12 — students who recall this case may associate it with the Ajay Hasia test, conflating the two.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a) — Pradeep Kumar Biswas (2002) refined the multi-factor test but did not establish the original six-factor test — that was Ajay Hasia (1981). The pair is incorrectly matched.

Eliminate (b) — Sukhdev Singh v. Bhagatram (1975) held that statutory corporations (LIC, ONGC, IFC) are 'State' under Article 12, but the multi-factor 'instrumentality test' was articulated in Ajay Hasia, not Sukhdev Singh.
Eliminate (c) — Ramana Dayaram Shetty (1979) did identify criteria for State status but is not the single foundational case for the six-factor test that became standard.

Option (d) — Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib (1981) is correctly paired with the formulation of the multi-factor test for determining whether a body is an 'other authority' (instrumentality/agency of State) under Article 12.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap involves substituting Pradeep Kumar Biswas or Sukhdev Singh for Ajay Hasia. Both are real Article 12 cases, and all deal with the 'State' definition. Students who recall 'a 1970s/80s case established the multi-factor test for Article 12' but are imprecise about which case will make entity-swap errors. The Ajay Hasia case is specifically associated with the six-factor instrumentality test.
solution.final_explanation:
The definition of 'State' under Article 12 directly determines which bodies are bound by Article 13. The expansion of this definition through judicial interpretation has been one of the most important developments in Indian constitutional law.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Pradeep Kumar Biswas v. Indian Institute of Chemical Biology (2002) is a significant case that refined the multi-factor test, but it did not originally formulate it. Pradeep Kumar Biswas moved away from a rigid checklist toward a holistic assessment.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Sukhdev Singh v. Bhagatram (1975) held that statutory corporations are 'State' under Article 12 and their employees can enforce service conditions against them as fundamental rights. It did not formulate the multi-factor instrumentality test.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Ramana Dayaram Shetty v. International Airport Authority (1979) also contributed to the Article 12 jurisprudence on 'instrumentality', but the canonical six-factor test is attributed to Ajay Hasia.
• Option (d) — Correct: Ajay Hasia v. Khalid Mujib (1981) formulated the six factors to determine whether a body is an 'instrumentality or agency of the State': government shareholding, financial dependence on government, deep pervasive control, functions of public importance, government monopoly, etc.

Value Addition:
• The six Ajay Hasia factors are used as a checklist — no single factor is decisive.
• Even bodies not created by statute can be 'State' if they satisfy the Ajay Hasia test.
• The expansion of Article 12 'State' directly widens the scope of Article 13 — more bodies become bound by fundamental rights.

solution.concept_anchor: Partial vs complete inconsistency — degree of invalidity under Article 13

statement_analysis.statement: When a post-constitutional law is partially inconsistent with a fundamental right, the entire law is void under Article 13(2), since any level of inconsistency with a fundamental right taints the whole enactment.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 13 provides that a law is void 'to the extent of the inconsistency'. Partial inconsistency does not automatically void the entire law — only the inconsistent portion is void, while the rest may survive if severable.

statement_analysis.statement: The test of inconsistency under Article 13 requires that compliance with the law must make it completely impossible to exercise a fundamental right — any lesser interference with the right does not render the law void.
statement_analysis.reason: The test of inconsistency does not require complete impossibility of exercising the fundamental right. Even laws that substantially curtail or restrict the exercise of a fundamental right (without making it completely impossible) can be found inconsistent under Article 13.

statement_analysis.statement: A law that restricts a fundamental right in a manner that falls within a permissible limitation clause (such as those under Article 19(2)–(6)) is not 'inconsistent' with that fundamental right for purposes of Article 13.
statement_analysis.reason: Permissible restrictions under Articles 19(2) to 19(6) are constitutionally authorised constraints on the rights in Article 19(1). A law that restricts speech within the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) does not violate Article 19(1)(a) and hence is not 'inconsistent' under Article 13.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Statement 3 is the correctly stated proposition (a true statement). Students who conflate 'inconsistency' with 'any restriction' may wrongly mark Statement 3 as incorrect, thinking that any law restricting a fundamental right is inconsistent with it.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1 — Article 13 voids a law 'to the extent of inconsistency', not entirely. Partial inconsistency = partial invalidity + potential severability. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Test Statement 2 — 'completely impossible' is too high a threshold. Substantial restriction or curtailment of a fundamental right can constitute inconsistency. Statement 2 is incorrect.

Test Statement 3 — laws operating within permissible limitation clauses (e.g., Article 19(2)) are constitutionally authorised. They are not 'inconsistent' with the right in the Article 13 sense. Statement 3 is CORRECT — it is NOT an incorrect statement.
Only Statements 1 and 2 are incorrect — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap operates in Statement 1, which conflates partial inconsistency with complete invalidity. The phrase 'any level of inconsistency with a fundamental right taints the whole enactment' sounds logically rigorous, exploiting the assumption that constitutional protection is all-or-nothing. The actual Article 13(2) text uses 'to the extent of the inconsistency' — a proportionality approach that most students overlook.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the degree and effect of inconsistency under Article 13 requires careful reading of the constitutional text.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Article 13(2) makes a law void 'to the extent of the inconsistency'. This phrase is critical — it permits severability, allowing courts to excise only the offending portion and uphold the rest. The statement's claim that 'any level of inconsistency voids the entire law' is incorrect.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Indian constitutional jurisprudence does not require complete impossibility of exercising a fundamental right for invalidity. Substantial abridgment or restriction — falling below the threshold of permissible limitations — is sufficient. The 'completely impossible' standard would make Article 13 nearly toothless.
• Statement 3 — Correct (not an incorrect statement): This captures the essential interaction between Article 13 and limitation clauses. Fundamental rights are not absolute — Articles 19(2) to 19(6) permit the State to restrict freedoms on specified grounds (security, public order, morality, etc.). A law that operates within these boundaries is not 'inconsistent' with the right — it exercises the State's constitutionally granted power to regulate.

Value Addition:
• The phrase 'to the extent of inconsistency' in Article 13(1) and 13(2) is the statutory basis for the doctrine of partial invalidity.
• Proportionality review (increasingly applied by the Supreme Court) examines whether restrictions are proportionate — going beyond mere 'reasonable restriction' analysis.
• K.S. Puttaswamy (Privacy case, 2017) adopted a proportionality standard for reviewing restrictions on fundamental rights under Article 13.

solution.concept_anchor: FDs as interpretive tool — not diluting FRs under Article 13
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who know that Fundamental Duties can be 'used in interpreting laws' may infer that this means they can reduce the standard of protection under Article 13 — an overextension of the interpretive role.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a) — FDs are not justiciable and do not automatically override FRs. No constitutional provision grants FD-implementing laws exemption from Article 13.

Eliminate (c) — using FDs to interpret ambiguous statutes does not mean courts reduce FR protection. The interpretive role of FDs is additive (preferring FD-consistent interpretations), not subtractive (reducing FR standards).
Eliminate (d) — FDs have interpretive relevance and are not completely irrelevant to Article 13 analysis. The statement goes too far in the other direction.
Option (b) correctly states the balanced position: FDs can guide statutory interpretation but cannot dilute or override fundamental rights protected under Article 13.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The scope-extension trap in option (c) extends the legitimate interpretive role of Fundamental Duties to an illegitimate one — reducing the standard of FR protection. Courts do use FDs to prefer one interpretation of an ambiguous statute over another, but this interpretive role never overrides or reduces the fundamental right itself. The trap catches students who know FDs have 'some role' in Article 13 analysis but are not precise about the limits of that role.
solution.final_explanation:
Fundamental Duties under Article 51A have a specific and limited role in the context of Article 13 interpretation.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Laws made to enforce Fundamental Duties have no special immunity from Article 13 scrutiny. If such a law violates a fundamental right, it is void under Article 13(2) — the duty-enforcement purpose does not create an exception.
• Option (b) — Correct: The courts' consistent position is that while Fundamental Duties can inform the interpretation of ambiguous statutes (preferring FD-consistent readings), they cannot reduce the protection afforded by fundamental rights under Article 13. FDs are interpretive guides, not override mechanisms.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: This overstates the role of FDs. They guide interpretation of ambiguous provisions — courts may prefer an interpretation consistent with, say, Article 51A(g) (environmental protection) — but this does not mean the court reduces the standard required by the fundamental right.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Fundamental Duties are not wholly irrelevant to constitutional interpretation. The Supreme Court has referenced them when reading environmental protection into Article 21 and in other contexts where they reinforce rights.

Value Addition:
• Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) as Article 51A, containing ten duties (now eleven after the 86th Amendment, 2002 added duty regarding education).
• The 11th duty (Article 51A(k)) requires parents to provide education opportunities for children aged 6–14, added alongside the Right to Education Act framework.
• In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India environmental cases, Article 51A(g) (duty to protect environment) reinforced the right to a clean environment under Article 21.

solution.concept_anchor: Prospective overruling — Deep Chand and administrative dislocation prevention
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know that both A and R are correct will need to carefully evaluate whether 'avoiding chaos' is actually why courts use prospective overruling (it is), making option (a) correct but option (b) the default choice for those who second-guess the causal link.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) factually correct? A states that courts occasionally declare laws invalid with prospective effect rather than ab initio, to prevent disruption to settled transactions and administrative arrangements. This is correct — prospective overruling/invalidation is an established, though exceptional, judicial tool used precisely to prevent the chaos of retrospective invalidity.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) factually correct? R states that the doctrine of eclipse applies only to pre-constitutional laws and renders them inoperative rather than void. This is correct — the doctrine of eclipse is exclusively for pre-constitutional laws under Article 13(1).

Step 3: Does R explain A? A is about prospective invalidation of post-constitutional laws. R is about eclipse of pre-constitutional laws. These are distinct doctrines addressing distinct categories of laws. The fact that eclipse exists for pre-constitutional laws does not explain why courts use prospective invalidation for post-constitutional laws. R does not causally explain A.
A is correct, R is correct, but R does NOT explain A — correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both A and R are true statements about Article 13 doctrines, but they deal with entirely different categories. The trap is that students may see 'pre-constitutional laws rendered inoperative rather than void' as somehow being the reason for prospective overruling — confusing 'not making laws dead' with 'making invalidity prospective'. These are different mechanisms applied to different situations. The causal link between them is absent.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests whether students understand the precise relationship between two different tools courts use when dealing with unconstitutional laws.

Assertion (A): CORRECT. Courts do use prospective invalidation — declaring a law invalid from the date of the judgment rather than from the date of enactment. This prevents the chaos of treating years of administrative actions and settled transactions as void. Deep Chand v. State of U.P. is a case associated with this principle, and it was explicitly used in Golak Nath as well.

Reason (R): CORRECT. The doctrine of eclipse applies exclusively to pre-constitutional laws under Article 13(1). Such laws become inoperative (eclipsed) rather than void — they lie dormant and can revive when the constitutional barrier (the fundamental right) is removed. Bhikaji Narain Dhakras established this.

Causal Link: ABSENT. A deals with how courts treat post-constitutional laws when declaring them invalid (prospective vs. retrospective). R deals with how pre-constitutional laws are treated by the Constitution itself (eclipse rather than void). These are independent doctrines operating on different categories of law. R does not explain why courts choose prospective invalidation for post-constitutional laws.

Correct option: (b).

Value Addition:
• Prospective overruling was formally introduced in Indian law in the Golak Nath judgment itself (1967) — an irony since the case concerned a constitutional amendment, not a statute.
• The doctrine of eclipse works automatically by constitutional operation; prospective overruling requires a deliberate judicial choice.
• De Facto Doctrine protects actions taken under laws later invalidated, serving a similar purpose to prospective overruling — both prevent retrospective chaos.

(b) Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A

solution.concept_anchor: Marbury v. Madison parallel — US vs Indian judicial review
solution.strong_distractor: b — Minerva Mills is associated with fundamental rights, the 42nd Amendment, and Article 13 — students may treat it as belonging to a different category than the others, whereas it actually squarely falls in the 'Article 13 and judicial review' category.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: cases that directly shaped the scope or exercise of judicial review under Article 13 or its equivalent.
Marbury v. Madison (1803) — established judicial review of legislative action; the US equivalent of Article 13. Belongs to the group.

Minerva Mills (1980) — exercised judicial review to strike down portions of the 42nd Amendment that curtailed judicial review itself. Directly related to Article 13's judicial review power. Belongs to the group.
L. Chandra Kumar (1997) — held that judicial review is a basic structure feature; the power cannot be taken away by Parliament. Directly about judicial review. Belongs to the group.
Maneka Gandhi (1978) — expanded Article 21's 'procedure established by law' to include fairness, but did not directly address judicial review power or Article 13 specifically. The odd one out.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Maneka Gandhi (1978) is an extremely important constitutional case — but it is primarily about the substantive content of 'procedure established by law' under Article 21, expanding personal liberty. It did not address the power or scope of judicial review under Article 13. Students who associate all landmark fundamental rights cases with Article 13 judicial review will incorrectly keep Maneka Gandhi in the group and eliminate a case that directly dealt with judicial review power.
solution.final_explanation:
Three of the four cases directly shaped the power, scope, or preservation of judicial review under Article 13 or its equivalent.

• Marbury v. Madison (1803): Established the doctrine of judicial review — that courts can strike down legislation inconsistent with constitutional provisions. This is the US parallel to India's Article 13 and frequently cited as the foundational precedent.
• Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980): Struck down clauses of the 42nd Amendment that attempted to immunise constitutional amendments from judicial review. The Supreme Court held that judicial review is a basic structure feature — Parliament cannot curtail it.
• L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997): Affirmed that judicial review is part of the basic structure and Parliament cannot take it away — even by constitutional amendment.
• Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978): This is the odd one out. This landmark case expanded the content of Article 21 by holding that 'procedure established by law' must be fair, just, and reasonable. It did not directly address the power of judicial review under Article 13.

Value Addition:
• After Maneka Gandhi, 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 is read as equivalent to 'due process of law' in the US Constitution.
• Minerva Mills is a direct consequence of Parliament's attempt to override Kesavananda Bharati through the 42nd Amendment.
• L. Chandra Kumar also held that jurisdiction of High Courts and Supreme Court under Articles 226 and 32 cannot be ousted.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 13 — all four sub-clauses tested together

statement_analysis.statement: Article 13(1) applies to 'laws in force' before the commencement of the Constitution, while Article 13(2) applies to laws made after the Constitution came into effect.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the fundamental temporal distinction in Article 13 — Article 13(1) governs pre-constitutional laws and subjects them to the doctrine of eclipse, while Article 13(2) governs post-constitutional laws making them void ab initio.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 13(4) was part of the original Constitution as adopted in 1949 and specifically protected constitutional amendments from the scope of Article 13 from the very beginning.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 13(4) was NOT in the original Constitution. It was inserted by the 24th Constitutional Amendment in 1971 specifically to counteract the Supreme Court's ruling in Golak Nath (1967) which had held that amendments are 'law' under Article 13.

statement_analysis.statement: The definition of 'law' in Article 13(3) excludes ordinary statutes passed by Parliament or State legislatures, covering only subordinate legislative instruments such as orders, rules, and notifications.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 13(3) provides an inclusive (not exhaustive) definition that adds items not ordinarily considered 'law'. Ordinary parliamentary and state legislation is inherently 'law' under Article 13 — the definition in Article 13(3) additionally captures delegated legislation, ordinances, customs, usages etc. It does not exclude statutes.

statement_analysis.statement: Article 13 as a whole serves as the constitutional foundation for judicial review of legislative action in India.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 13 is universally recognised as the textual foundation of judicial review in India — it expressly declares inconsistent laws void and impliedly confers on courts the power to make such declarations.

solution.strong_distractor: c — 'Only three' attracts students who correctly identify Statements 1 and 4 as correct and Statement 3 as incorrect, but then incorrectly mark Statement 2 as correct (not knowing about the 24th Amendment insertion history), giving them three correct statements.
elimination_logic: Confirm Statement 1 — pre-constitutional (13(1)) vs post-constitutional (13(2)) distinction is accurately stated. Correct.
Test Statement 2 — Article 13(4) was inserted by the 24th Amendment (1971), not in the original Constitution. The original Constitution did not have this clause. Incorrect.
Test Statement 3 — Article 13(3) is inclusive, not exclusive of ordinary statutes. Statutes are inherently 'law'; 13(3) adds more. The statement inverting this — excluding statutes — is incorrect.
Confirm Statement 4 — Article 13 is the foundation of judicial review in India. Correct. Two statements (1 and 4) are correct — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the assumption that a provision as important as Article 13(4) must have been in the original Constitution — students who have not studied constitutional amendment history may accept this as self-evident. In fact, Parliament had to specifically amend the Constitution in 1971 to add this protection, after the Supreme Court's Golak Nath ruling created a constitutional crisis.
solution.final_explanation:
A comprehensive test of all four sub-clauses of Article 13.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The temporal division between Article 13(1) (pre-constitutional laws → eclipse) and 13(2) (post-constitutional laws → void ab initio) is the foundational structure of the Article.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Article 13(4) was not part of the original Constitution. The Constituent Assembly did not include it. It was inserted by the 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 — Parliament's response to Golak Nath v. State of Punjab (1967), which had held amendments to be 'law' challengeable under Article 13.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Article 13(3) provides an inclusive definition that supplements (not replaces) the ordinary meaning of 'law'. Statutes passed by Parliament or State legislatures are 'law' under Article 13 even without being listed in Article 13(3). The sub-clause additionally captures ordinances, notifications, rules, bye-laws, customs, and usages.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Article 13 is the explicit textual foundation for judicial review of legislation in India — unlike the US where Marbury v. Madison inferred this power from the constitutional structure.

Value Addition:
• Article 13 is in Part III (Fundamental Rights) — its placement means it is itself immune from simple parliamentary amendment (subject to basic structure).
• The original Constitution's Article 13 had only three clauses (now renumbered); the fourth was added in 1971.
• Judicial review under Article 13 is available in the Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226).

solution.concept_anchor: Triple Talaq — Article 13 and personal law customs
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know that Article 13(3) includes customs and usages will be drawn toward (a), not appreciating that the Narasu controversy creates uncertainty about whether 'personal laws' (as distinct from customs) are 'law' under Article 13, and that the Shayara Bano case avoided deciding this.
elimination_logic: Identify the scenario: a religious personal law practice (not a statute) is being challenged on fundamental rights grounds.
Eliminate (b) — the State is not the direct party here; the practice is personal law, not a State-enacted law. The challenge must address whether personal law practices are 'law' under Article 13.
Eliminate (c) — Article 13 does not automatically apply to personal law practices as the Narasu controversy demonstrates; the legal position is not settled in the way (c) suggests.

Eliminate (a) — while (a) is partially true (customs are within Article 13(3)), the specific position on personal laws (as distinct from customs) is contested. The Supreme Court in Shayara Bano avoided deciding whether personal law is 'law' under Article 13, instead using Article 14's manifest arbitrariness test.
Option (d) correctly states the nuanced position: the challenge is possible under Article 14 without conclusively resolving the Narasu controversy about personal law and Article 13.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The partial-truth trap in option (a) exploits Article 13(3)'s explicit inclusion of customs. A practice rooted in religious personal law may be characterised as a 'custom', bringing it arguably within Article 13. But the Supreme Court in Shayara Bano deliberately did not resolve whether Muslim personal law is 'law' under Article 13 — instead using the manifest arbitrariness test under Article 14. Option (a) overstates the legal clarity on this point.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario mirrors the Shayara Bano (Triple Talaq) case and tests the legal architecture for challenging personal law practices.

The governing complexity: Article 13(3) includes customs and usages having force of law. However, the Narasu Appa Mali case (Bombay HC, 1952) held that personal law as such is NOT 'law' under Article 13 — a position never definitively overruled by the Supreme Court.

• Option (a) — Incorrect (oversimplified): While customs with force of law are within Article 13(3), whether religious personal law practices qualify as 'customs having force of law' under Article 13 is contested. The Supreme Court in Shayara Bano avoided this question.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The scenario involves a personal law practice, not a State-enacted statute. A simple writ against the 'State' under Article 13 does not fit this scenario cleanly.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Personal law practices are not automatically immune from all constitutional challenge — they can be challenged under Article 14 (manifest arbitrariness) as the Shayara Bano case demonstrated.
• Option (d) — Correct: A fundamental rights challenge can proceed under Article 14 (manifest arbitrariness) even without resolving whether the practice is 'law' under Article 13. The Supreme Court in Shayara Bano (2017) struck down instant triple talaq as manifestly arbitrary under Article 14, deliberately leaving the Narasu controversy undecided.

Value Addition:
• The POSH Act (2013) and Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 demonstrate how legislative action resolves ambiguities that courts avoid.
• Article 14's manifest arbitrariness test (Shayara Bano, 2017) has become a powerful alternative to Article 13 challenges in personal law contexts.
• The Law Commission has repeatedly flagged the Narasu controversy as an unresolved constitutional question.

(b) The challenge cannot proceed under Article 13 because the practice is not enacted by the 'State' and therefore falls entirely outside the constitutional challenge framework
(c) Personal law practices are immune from fundamental rights challenge and the court must dismiss the petition at the threshold

solution.concept_anchor: FDs — non-enforceability cannot override FRs; 11th FD added by 86th Amendment

statement_analysis.statement: The eleven Fundamental Duties in Article 51A include a duty on parents and guardians to provide opportunities for education to their children between the ages of six and fourteen years, added by the Eighty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment (2002).
statement_analysis.reason: The 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) added Article 51A(k) — the duty of parents and guardians to provide educational opportunities to children aged 6–14 — as the eleventh Fundamental Duty, alongside inserting Article 21-A (Right to Education).

statement_analysis.statement: A law enacted to enforce the Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(g) — to protect and improve the natural environment — cannot be challenged under Article 13 on the ground that it restricts a fundamental right, since Fundamental Duties have the same constitutional standing as Fundamental Rights.
statement_analysis.reason: Fundamental Duties do not have the same constitutional standing as Fundamental Rights and cannot immunise laws from Article 13 scrutiny. No provision of the Constitution grants laws enforcing FDs special exemption from fundamental rights challenge. Laws enforcing FDs remain fully subject to Article 13.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know both facts independently — the 86th Amendment and the interpretive role of FDs — may mark both as correct without noticing that Statement 2 overstates the constitutional standing of Fundamental Duties.
elimination_logic: Test Statement 1 — the 86th Amendment (2002) added Article 51A(k) and Article 21-A (Right to Education). The eleventh FD relates to parental duty regarding education. Statement 1 is correct.

Test Statement 2 — the claim that FDs have 'the same constitutional standing as Fundamental Rights' and can immunise laws from Article 13 is fabricated. No constitutional text supports this. FDs are non-justiciable and create no exemption from Article 13. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 contains a plausible-fabrication trap: the assertion that Fundamental Duties have 'the same constitutional standing as Fundamental Rights' sounds constitutional in its language but has no basis. The Constitution places FDs in Part IV-A, makes them non-justiciable, and provides no mechanism by which they override fundamental rights. The fabrication is designed to catch students who know FDs are 'important' but do not know their precise constitutional hierarchy.
solution.final_explanation:
The Fundamental Duties in Article 51A have a specific and bounded constitutional role that must not be conflated with the legal standing of Fundamental Rights.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 86th Constitutional Amendment (2002) added Article 51A(k) as the eleventh Fundamental Duty — the obligation of every parent/guardian to provide educational opportunities to children in the 6–14 age group. This was simultaneously enacted with Article 21-A (Right to Education) and the Right to Education Act framework.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: This statement fabricates a constitutional equivalence that does not exist. Fundamental Duties are in Part IV-A (not Part III) and are non-justiciable. No constitutional provision creates a hierarchy where FDs equal FRs or exempts FD-enforcing laws from Article 13 scrutiny. Courts have consistently held that laws must independently satisfy Article 13 regardless of their FD-enforcement purpose.

Correct answer: Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect — option (c).

Value Addition:
• Original Article 51A (42nd Amendment, 1976) contained ten duties. The 86th Amendment (2002) added the eleventh — Article 51A(k).
• The Verma Committee report (1999) recommended operationalising FDs through legislation — the 86th Amendment partly implemented this.
• Article 21-A (Right to Education) and the RTE Act, 2009 were enabled by the same 86th Amendment that added Article 51A(k).

solution.concept_anchor: Minerva Mills — executive actions challengeable under Article 13
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Minerva Mills is a landmark Article 13 case about the 42nd Amendment may associate it only with constitutional amendments and not recall that it also addressed executive actions under Article 13.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (b) — Minerva Mills did address the 42nd Amendment but also specifically dealt with executive actions under Article 13, not just constitutional amendments. Option (b) narrows the holding too much.

Eliminate (c) — Minerva Mills did not hold that executive actions require explicit statutory backing to be challenged under Article 13. Executive actions can also be challenged as arbitrary under Article 14 independently.
Eliminate (d) — Minerva Mills did not restrict Article 13 application to Parliament only; State executive actions are also within Article 13's scope through Article 12.

Option (a) correctly captures the Minerva Mills principle: executive actions that have the force of law can be challenged under Article 13, and the case affirmed this alongside its constitutional amendment holdings.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap operates by attributing the Minerva Mills holding to other cases or by limiting its scope to only the 42nd Amendment aspects. Minerva Mills is multi-layered — it addressed both constitutional amendments (basic structure) and the independence of executive action from Article 13 scrutiny. Candidates who know Minerva Mills only from its Basic Structure dimension will be confused.
solution.final_explanation:
Minerva Mills Ltd. v. Union of India (1980) is a multi-dimensional constitutional judgment with implications for both legislative and executive action under Article 13.

• Option (a) — Correct: The Minerva Mills case affirmed that executive actions having the force of law are subject to challenge under Article 13. The Court maintained the principle that no arm of the State — including the executive — can override fundamental rights through actions that constitute 'law' under Article 13(3).
• Option (b) — Incorrect (too narrow): While Minerva Mills famously struck down clauses 4 and 5 of the 42nd Amendment for violating the basic structure (by immunising constitutional amendments from judicial review and expanding Article 31-C), this is not its only holding. Limiting the case to constitutional amendments misses its broader executive action jurisprudence.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Minerva Mills did not impose a requirement of explicit statutory backing as a precondition for challenging executive actions under Article 13. Actions with force of law are covered regardless of whether they are statutory.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Article 13 applies to laws made by the 'State' as defined in Article 12, which includes State governments and their executives, not just Parliament.

Value Addition:
• Minerva Mills struck down Section 55 (inserting Article 368(4) and (5)) and Section 4 (expanding Article 31-C) of the 42nd Amendment.
• The case affirmed that a limited amending power and judicial review are both features of the basic structure.
• Minerva Mills is often taught alongside Kesavananda Bharati as the two-phase establishment of the Basic Structure doctrine.

formatted_presentation.display_text:
Which of the following most accurately reflects the significance of the Minerva Mills case in the context of Article 13's application to executive actions?

(a) The case affirmed that executive actions having the force of law remain subject to challenge under Article 13, and no provision of law — whether legislative or executive — can override fundamental rights by virtue of being government-directed
(b) The case confined Article 13's application exclusively to constitutional amendments and held that executive actions fall outside Article 13's scope, being separately governed by Article 14
(c) The case held that executive actions can be challenged under Article 13 only if they are backed by explicit statutory authority — purely discretionary executive orders are beyond Article 13
(d) The case restricted the application of Article 13 to laws made by Parliament alone, exempting State government executive actions from its ambit

solution.concept_anchor: Union Territory laws — subject to Article 13 through Article 12
solution.strong_distractor: d — Students may believe that 'Parliament and State legislatures' is the complete answer since these are the two main legislative bodies named in most Article 13 discussions, not noticing that Union Territory legislatures (through Article 12 and the 'local or other authority' category) are also covered.
elimination_logic: The blank requires identification of which legislative bodies are subject to Article 13.
Eliminate (a) — 'Parliament alone' is far too narrow; state legislatures are clearly covered.
Eliminate (c) — 'Parliament and State legislatures only' excludes Union Territory legislatures which are also within 'State' under Article 12.

Eliminate (d) — 'Parliament, State legislatures, and private corporations' — private corporations are not legislative bodies making 'law' in the Article 13(3) sense; they are separate Article 12 question.
Option (b) — 'Parliament, State legislatures, and Union Territory legislatures with legislative power' — correctly captures all legislative bodies whose output is 'law' subject to Article 13.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The geographic-swap trap operates by making students assume that only the two main legislative bodies (Parliament and State legislatures) are mentioned in Article 13 discussions, causing them to overlook Union Territory legislatures. Jammu & Kashmir (post-2019) and Puducherry are Union Territories with legislatures — their laws are equally subject to Article 13. The complete answer requires recognising all three categories of legislatures.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 13's prohibition operates against laws made by all legislative authorities within the 'State' under Article 12.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Restricting Article 13 to Parliament alone is clearly wrong — state laws are expressly and routinely subject to Article 13 challenge in High Courts and the Supreme Court.
• Option (b) — Correct: Article 13 applies to laws made by Parliament, State legislatures, and Union Territory legislatures that have been granted legislative power. Currently, Jammu & Kashmir and Puducherry have legislatures. Their laws are subject to Article 13 on the same basis as state laws, through the definition of 'State' in Article 12.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: This excludes Union Territory legislatures. The 'Parliament and State legislatures only' answer is incomplete given that UTs with legislatures also have law-making power subject to Article 13.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Private corporations do not make 'law' in the legislative sense used in Article 13(3). Their internal regulations may be subject to fundamental rights challenge if they are 'State' under Article 12, but this is through Article 12, not through their being 'law-making bodies' for Article 13 purposes.

Value Addition:
• Article 239A (for Puducherry) and Article 239AA (for Delhi) specifically grant legislative competence to these UTs.
• Delhi's legislature (GNCT) makes laws subject to Article 13 in the same manner as state legislatures.
• Extra-territorial laws (laws with effects outside India) can also be challenged under Article 13 if they affect fundamental rights of persons within India.

(d) Parliament, State legislatures, and private corporations performing public functions, since all three qualify as 'State' under Article 12

solution.concept_anchor: Presumption of constitutionality — reading down preferred over striking down
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who identify both A and R as correct will likely conclude they are causally connected since both deal with how courts approach constitutional challenges, making option (a) seem obvious.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? A states that courts prefer to 'read down' (interpret narrowly) a law to save it rather than strike it down entirely when faced with a constitutional challenge. This is correct — reading down is a fundamental judicial technique flowing from the presumption of constitutionality.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? R states that the burden of proving a law unconstitutional lies on the challenger. This is correct — the presumption of constitutionality means the law is presumed valid and the challenger must discharge the burden.

Step 3: Does R explain A? The reason courts prefer reading down over striking down is the principle of constitutional parsimony and the presumption of constitutionality — they should minimise the invalidation of legislative choices. While R (burden on challenger) and A (preference for reading down) both stem from the same root principle, R does NOT causally explain A. The preference for reading down is a judicial philosophy about minimising invalidation; it exists independently of who bears the burden of proof. A court can prefer reading down even after the challenger has discharged the burden — the two operate at different stages and levels.
A correct, R correct, R does NOT explain A — correct option is (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Both A and R flow from the same overarching principle — the presumption of constitutionality — which makes option (a) very tempting. However, the causal relationship is absent: who bears the burden of proof (R) does not cause courts to prefer reading down (A). They are parallel consequences of the same underlying principle, not a cause-effect pair. Distinguishing 'same root, different branches' from 'cause and effect' is the core skill this question tests.
solution.final_explanation:
Both the preference for reading down and the burden of proof placement are judicial principles that stem from the presumption of constitutionality — but they are parallel consequences, not causally linked.

Assertion (A): CORRECT. 'Reading down' (or 'reading down to save') is a well-established technique: when a law can be interpreted either constitutionally or unconstitutionally, courts choose the constitutional interpretation and narrow the law's scope to preserve it. This avoids the drastic remedy of striking down an entire legislative act.

Reason (R): CORRECT. The presumption of constitutionality places the initial burden on the challenger. The State does not need to prove its law is valid — validity is presumed unless the challenger demonstrates inconsistency with a fundamental right.

Causal Link: ABSENT. R explains why the challenger must bring evidence, not why courts prefer reading down. The preference for reading down is a judicial policy of constitutional parsimony — separating the valid from the invalid wherever possible. This exists whether or not the challenger has met their burden. After the challenger successfully shows prima facie invalidity, courts still prefer reading down over striking down where possible — a choice independent of the burden allocation.

Correct option: (b).

Value Addition:
• Reading down was applied in State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952) — one of the first cases on reasonable restrictions.
• Courts distinguish reading down (saving a law by narrowing scope) from reading in (adding words to make a law constitutional — rarely done).
• The manifest arbitrariness test (Shayara Bano, 2017) raises the standard at which the burden shifts, but does not change the structure of the burden.
